response.sql: WITH g AS (SELECT p.SEX, COUNT(DISTINCT e.ID) AS cnt FROM Examination e JOIN Patient p ON p.ID = e.ID GROUP BY p.SEX), s AS (SELECT SEX, cnt, cnt * 1.0 / SUM(cnt) OVER () AS share, AVG(cnt) OVER () AS avg_cnt FROM g) SELECT SUM(cnt) AS combined_total, AVG(share) AS avg_share, AVG(cnt - avg_cnt) AS avg_above_average FROM s WHERE cnt > avg_cnt

assumptions.assumption: 'How many were examined' counts distinct patients with at least one examination per sex, not examination records. The overall total is the sum of the per-sex counts. Since each patient has one sex, this equals the number of distinct examined patients.
NULL and empty-string SEX values are kept as two separate groups, and each counts as a 'sex' when computing the per-sex average.

The per-sex average is the mean of the per-sex counts. 'Average share' is the mean of the above-average sexes' shares of the overall total. 'How far above' is the mean of (count minus per-sex average count) for those sexes, in count units.
Examinations are linked to patients by an inner join on ID, so examinations with a NULL ID are excluded.

alternatives.interpretation: Count examination records per sex rather than distinct patients, so a patient with several examinations counts several times.
alternatives.sql: WITH g AS (SELECT p.SEX, COUNT(*) AS cnt FROM Examination e JOIN Patient p ON p.ID = e.ID GROUP BY p.SEX), s AS (SELECT SEX, cnt, cnt * 1.0 / SUM(cnt) OVER () AS share, AVG(cnt) OVER () AS avg_cnt FROM g) SELECT SUM(cnt) AS combined_total, AVG(share) AS avg_share, AVG(cnt - avg_cnt) AS avg_above_average FROM s WHERE cnt > avg_cnt
